Could first tithe also cease then?
Rabbi Yehuda cites the continuing duty to give the Levite his portion.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya’akov instead cites the inheritance comparison to keep first tithe continuous.
A vow barring benefit for a year lasts twelve full months from its date.
A vow for “this year” expires at Tishrei, even if begun on the last day of Elul.
A single day suffices here even for a view requiring more for a legal year, because the promised hardship has occurred.

A mishna sets tithe maturity at sprouting for fenugreek and one-third growth for grain and olives.
What kind of sprouting is meant?
The fenugreek has developed seeds capable of sprouting.
The one-third threshold for grain and olives is recalled.
What is the source for that threshold?
Rav Asi transmits a reading of the Sabbatical-year verse.
The verse places “year of release” alongside Sukkot.
Sukkot is already in the eighth year, so why call it a Sabbatical-year occasion?

13a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Perhaps the Sabbatical rule simply continues to Sukkot even for produce that had not grown in year seven.

Does gathering merely describe the festival season, already stated elsewhere in the verse?
Gathering means harvest: grain cut at Sukkot had reached one-third growth before Rosh Hashanah.
Can the Sages really distinguish one-third growth from slightly less?
Rabbi Zeira insists that legal measures have exact boundaries.
A ritual bath with forty se’a works, but one a tiny amount short does not.
An egg-bulk of food transmits impurity, but one short by a sesame seed does not.
A cloth three by three handbreadths is susceptible to treading impurity; one short by a hair is not.
Rabbi Yirmeya retracts his objection by recalling a question posed to Rav Kahana.
Where did Israel obtain the omer offering upon entering the Land?
Gentile-owned grain seems unfit because the Torah requires “your harvest.”
Perhaps no omer offering was brought that year.
They ate new grain only after Passover, implying that the omer was first offered.
What grain, then, did they bring?
Rav Kahana identifies grain that had not reached one-third growth under gentile ownership.
Rabbi Yirmeya argues this example shows they could tell whether grain passed one-third growth.
Perhaps the grain had not grown at all under gentile ownership, leaving no close measurement.

Even grain already one-quarter grown would have to mature improbably quickly in five days.
The Land’s exceptional fertility could explain such rapid ripening in either case.
Rabbi Ḥanina challenges the claim that gathering at Sukkot means harvesting; another verse refers to collected threshing and winepress waste.
Rabbi Zeira concedes that this objection defeats the earlier proof.
What then establishes the one-third growth rule?
Rabbi Yonatan ben Yosef introduces a verse about yield for three years; the derivation continues on 13b.

13b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: “For three” is read as “for one-third,” supporting the growth threshold.
The phrase may be needed for its plain promise of three years’ yield.
A second verse supplies that promise, leaving this wording available for the one-third reading.
Rice, millet, poppy, and sesame follow the year when they root, including for tithes and Sabbatical law.
Rabba asks which standard applies to these crops when trees, grain, olives, and vegetables have different thresholds.
Because they ripen in batches, the Sages use rooting as a common date for the field.
Abaye proposes mixing the harvest, so new produce is tithed for new and old for old.
A baraita forbids cross-year tithing when Egyptian cowpea plants rooted on opposite sides of Rosh Hashanah.
How can those cowpeas then be tithed?
Mix the harvest thoroughly and take tithes proportionately from old and new portions.
Rabba says Rabbi Shimon Shezuri accepts reliable mixing, whereas the Sages do not.
Shmuel nevertheless rules like Rabbi Yosei ben Keifar’s report of Rabbi Shimon Shezuri.
Rabbi Zeira cites Shmuel’s separate denial of reliable mixing except in wine and oil.
Shmuel’s ruling can rest on the crop’s full ripening date rather than on mixing.

14a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Shmuel’s ruling for Rabbi Shimon Shezuri alone might wrongly suggest he accepts mixing of solids.
His rejection of general mixing alone might wrongly suggest he rules with the opposing Sages.
Together those claims seem contradictory, so his full-ripening rule explains the ruling.
The ruling for beans limits that ripening rule; grain and olives still follow one-third growth.
Why also state that mixing generally fails?
That statement preserves the exception for wine and oil.
Rabbi Yosei HaGelili uses the threshing-floor verse to distinguish crops nourished by the old year’s rain from vegetables nourished by new rain.
Rabbi Akiva instead distinguishes rain-fed crops from vegetables needing irrigation.
What practical difference follows from their readings?
Rabbi Abbahu identifies seedless onions and Egyptian cowpeas.
When watering stops thirty days before Rosh Hashanah they follow the old year; otherwise they follow the new one.
The discussion turns to Shevat as the new year for trees.
Why set the tree date then?
Most annual rain has already fallen, though most of the winter season remains.
How is that statement to be understood?
The rain threshold makes a new produce year despite the winter still ahead.
A baraita reports Rabbi Akiva taking two tithes from an etrog picked on the first of Shevat.

14b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: One tithe follows Beit Shammai’s first-of-Shevat date and the other Beit Hillel’s fifteenth-of-Shevat date.
Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda instead attributes Rabbi Akiva’s double tithe to differing views of Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer.
A mishna treats etrog as a tree for orla, fourth-year fruit, and Sabbatical law, but as a vegetable for its picking-based tithe year.
Rabbi Eliezer treats etrog as a tree for every purpose.
Can one simultaneously follow two authorities’ stringencies?
A baraita criticizes combining the opposing leniencies or stringencies of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel.
Instead, one follows a single school consistently.
Rabbi Akiva was unsure which Shevat date Beit Hillel actually taught, so he covered both possibilities.
The alternative account again attributes the double tithe to Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer.
Picking on the first of Shevat still seems to follow Beit Shammai.
The etrog had formed before the previous fifteenth of Shevat, allowing the picking and formation rules to yield different years.
An earlier picking could have made the same point, but the reported incident happened on this date.
Ravina emends the report to the fifteenth of Shevat and explains the two tithes through the etrog dispute.
Rabba bar Rav Huna infers that a picking-based etrog tithe year should begin in Tishrei, like vegetables.
A baraita instead separates etrog fruit picked before and after the fifteenth of Shevat sunset, forbidding cross-year tithing.

ranges.en: Rabban Gamliel follows picking for etrog tithe, yet the baraita still dates its new year to Shevat.

Why do vegetable and etrog baraitot use different adjacent years for their examples?
The etrog case incidentally teaches that handling the tree in the Sabbatical year impairs its fruit for three years.

Does he mean lunar Shevat or a solar-season date?
He means the lunar month.
Another inquiry asks whether a leap year changes that date.
The rule follows the usual years, leaving the date in Shevat.

Abaye says formation time explains the first exemption from elimination but seems to require tithe.
Rabba treats the fruit as ownerless after public handling, exempting it from tithe.
Rav Hamnuna assigns each etrog entirely to its formation year.

ranges.en: The repeated seated and standing shofar blasts confuse the accuser.

An unstable wall, excessive confidence in prayer, and appealing for judgment against another can recall one’s sins.

Charity, prayer, changing one’s name, and changing one’s conduct can undo a decree.

Another verse links cries to God with rescue from distress.

Nineveh’s changed deeds lead God to withdraw the threatened calamity.
Another view adds moving location, citing Abram’s journey and subsequent blessing.

Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina says God lifts the side of sins, citing a verse about bearing sin.

ranges.en: The mercy described applies to one who regards himself as a mere remnant.

Rabbi Yoḥanan reads God’s passing before Moses as teaching an order of prayer and mercy after sin.

Rav Yehuda cites a covenant that the thirteen attributes of mercy will not return empty.
Rabbi Yoḥanan uses Isaiah to argue that repentance can undo a decree.
Rav Pappa asks whether the verse concerns only repentance before a decree.
Abaye says healing implies a condition already imposed, namely an issued decree.

After a sparse rain decree, later repentance brings the rain at useful times and places.
After an abundant rain decree, later wrongdoing brings the rain at useless times and places.

The desired benefit can be achieved without changing the decreed amount.
The psalm about endangered sailors describes distress, prayer, rescue, and thanks.
Its textual markers suggest prayer after the decree may fail, challenging the communal exception.
Sailors are treated as individuals rather than the whole community.
Beloreya asks why one verse denies divine favoritism while another promises it.
Rabbi Yosei compares a debtor who can obtain a king’s pardon but must still repay or appease his lender.

Rabbi Akiva introduces another explanation, continued on 18a.

18a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Akiva distinguishes divine favor before a decree from judgment after it.

One prayed and was answered, while the other was not.
Why did their prayers receive different answers?
The answered prayer was wholehearted.
Rabbi Elazar instead distinguishes prayer before a decree from prayer after it.
Rabbi Yitzḥak says crying out can help both before and after a decree.
Two Jeremiah verses seem to make communal cleansing possible before a decree but impossible afterward.

The sworn judgment against Eli’s house supplies an example of a decree that cannot be undone by sacrifice.
Rava allows atonement through Torah study instead.
Abaye adds acts of kindness to Torah study.
Rabba and Abaye, descendants of Eli, lived forty and sixty years respectively under those differing practices.
A Jerusalem family facing early death was advised to study Torah and lived.
How is a community’s decree described as unsealed?
A verse explicitly calls its sin sealed.
Even a sealed communal decree can be torn up when the people call to God.
Another verse says to seek God only while He may be found.
That limit applies to an individual, not the whole community.
When is God especially near an individual?
During the ten days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur.
Why did Nabal’s death come ten days later?
One explanation credits ten meals he gave David’s servants.
Another makes the delay the ten days of opportunity for repentance.
What does the mishna mean by creatures passing like benei maron?
One explanation compares them to sheep.
Another compares them to travelers on the steep ascent of Beit Maron.
Another compares them to soldiers of David’s house.
Rabbi Yoḥanan says all are surveyed in one glance.
A verse about hearts and deeds is read as God viewing all hearts and acts at once.

18b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Zechariah calls four dated fasts future occasions of joy, prompting a question about their status.

Peace makes them joyous; its absence makes them fasts.

Its multiple calamities make that fast different, including both destructions, Beitar, and the plowing of Jerusalem.
Rabbi Shimon introduces his disagreement with Rabbi Akiva over the four fasts.
Rabbi Akiva identifies the fourth-month fast with the breach of Jerusalem in Tammuz.
He identifies the fifth-month fast with the Temple fire in Av.
He identifies the seventh-month fast with Gedaliah’s death in Tishrei, equating a righteous death with the Temple’s burning.
He identifies the tenth-month fast with the Babylonian siege in Tevet.
Why list the siege last although it happened first?
The prophet lists the months in order.
Rabbi Shimon instead identifies the tenth-month fast with news of Jerusalem’s fall reaching the exiles.

An Arab’s word for a load clarifies yehavkha in a psalm.
The mishna describes a straight ibex shofar and shorter trumpet blasts on Rosh HaShana.
For public fasts it describes curved ram horns and longer trumpet blasts.
Jubilee Yom Kippur shares the blasts and blessings; Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes its horn.
Rabbi Levi favors curved horns for Rosh HaShana and Jubilee Yom Kippur.
The mishna instead names a straight ibex horn for Rosh HaShana.
His Rosh HaShana position follows Rabbi Yehuda’s baraita.
Why not simply state that the law follows Rabbi Yehuda?
That would wrongly imply Rabbi Levi also accepts his Jubilee horn rule.
What principle divides the two opinions?
Rabbi Yehuda favors a bowed posture on Rosh HaShana and a straight one on Yom Kippur.
The other tanna favors straightness on Rosh HaShana and humility on fast days.

27a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna’s gold-plated shofar mouth is recalled.
A baraita disqualifies gold plating at the place touched by the mouth.
Abaye places the mishna’s plating above that contact point.
The two accompanying trumpets are recalled.
A baraita about two simultaneous utterances suggests that the ear cannot distinguish both sounds.
The shofar blast is prolonged.
This seems to assume that hearing only part of a blast fulfills the duty.
A mishna counts one elongated blast as only one, not two.
Why can it not count as two if a partial blast suffices?
One continuous blast cannot be split into two blasts.
A mishna distinguishes a clear shofar sound from an echo in a pit or vessel.
Why not fulfill the duty from the clear beginning before the echo?
The revised distinction is between two sounds from one source and sounds from separate sources.
Torah reading rules appear to bar two simultaneous readers or translators.
Beloved readings such as Hallel allow listeners to attend to multiple voices, as with shofar.
Why prolong the shofar blast, then?
It signals that the shofar is the day’s central mitzva.
The silver plating of fast-day shofarot is recalled.
Why use gold on Rosh HaShana but silver on fast days?
One answer cites the silver trumpets used to summon an assembly.
Another answer says the Torah spares communal expense.
On that reasoning, Rosh HaShana should also use silver.
Honoring the festival takes priority.
Rav Pappa bar Shmuel plans to use both instruments as the mishna describes.
Rava limits that combined practice to the Temple.
A baraita distinguishes the Temple from places that use either shofar or trumpets.
Two sages are reported to have combined the instruments in their towns.
The Sages say that combination belonged only at the Temple’s eastern gates and Mount.
What verse supports that limit?
The psalm joins trumpets and shofar specifically before the Lord, the King.
The mishna’s comparison between Jubilee and Rosh HaShana is recalled.
Whose view underlies the prayer calling Rosh HaShana the beginning of creation?
It follows Rabbi Eliezer, who places creation in Tishrei.
Rav Eina objects that the creation line cannot be said on Jubilee Yom Kippur.
The mishna compares the other portions of the blessings.
An alternate teaching asks whose view supports the mishna’s equal blessings.
It seems unlike Rabbi Eliezer because the creation line fits Rosh HaShana alone.
Again the comparison covers the remaining blessings.
The next mishna disqualifies a repaired cracked shofar or one joined from fragments.

27b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna distinguishes a sealed puncture that hinders the blast from one that does not.
A listener in a pit or vessel must hear the shofar itself rather than an echo.
A listener near a synagogue fulfills the duty only if the hearing is accompanied by intent.
A baraita permits shortening or scraping a shofar.
It distinguishes plating at the mouthpiece, inside, and outside according to its effect.
It repeats the puncture rule based on whether blowing is hindered.
With one shofar inside another, the inner sound alone fulfills the duty.
Another baraita permits scraping, distinguishes nested horns, and rejects an inverted horn.
Rav Pappa explains inversion as reversing the narrow and wide ends.
The verse requires blowing in the horn’s natural direction.
The mishna’s rule against glued fragments is recalled.
A baraita disqualifies any addition to the shofar.
The baraita and Rabbi Natan differ over sealing a hole with matching material.
One version of Rabbi Yoḥanan requires most of the original horn to remain.
By inference, a foreign patch fails even when most of the original remains.
Another version limits disqualification by a foreign patch to a mostly missing horn.
By inference, a matching patch works even when most of the horn was missing.
Inside gold plating invalidates; outside plating depends on whether the sound changes.
A lengthwise crack invalidates; a widthwise crack depends on the remaining sounding length.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel defines that length by what protrudes past both sides of a hand.
High, deep, and rough sounds are all acceptable shofar sounds.
A report to Shmuel’s father permits a horn whose inside was drilled.
Why state this when ordinary shofarot are drilled?
Rav Ashi says even drilling through the horn’s inner bone does not interpose.
The mishna’s pit and cistern rule is recalled.
Rav Huna distinguishes listeners at the edge, hearing echo, from listeners inside.
A baraita says a listener can fulfill the duty when the blast is sounded into a pit.
How does that fit the mishna’s contrary ruling?
The two sources fit Rav Huna’s distinction.
An alternate presentation directly contrasts the mishna and baraita.
Rav Huna resolves them by the listener’s location.
Rabba begins a further teaching on 28a.

28a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabba accepts a blast crossing the edge of a pit but not one crossing dawn.
Abaye asks why both cases do not require the entire blast in a valid setting.
Night is never a time of obligation, while the pit is valid for a listener inside it.
The ruling seems to treat the heard end or beginning of a blast as sufficient.
A mishna counts a prolonged blast as only one blast.
Why cannot it count as two?
A continuous blast cannot be divided.
A mishna disqualifies hearing an echo rather than the shofar.
Why not count the clear beginning before the echo?
Rabba concerns a blower who climbs from the pit while sounding for himself.
What new point does that teach?
Even if the horn remains briefly in the pit as his head emerges, he fulfills the duty.
Rav Yehuda distinguishes blowing a horn of a burnt-offering from one of a peace-offering.
Why distinguish them?
Misuse removes the burnt-offering’s sanctity, whereas the peace-offering’s prohibition remains.
Rava objects that misuse would occur only after sounding, too late to validate the blast.
Rava first concludes that neither horn fulfills the duty.
He later reverses himself: both do, because mitzvot are not given as personal benefit.
Rav Yehuda distinguishes a shofar used for idolatry from one from an idolatrous city.
The city’s objects are legally treated as destroyed and lacking the needed measure.
Rava permits a mitzva blast despite vows barring benefit from the blower or horn.
He permits purification and immersion under such vows in the rainy season, when there is no cooling benefit.
A report says a person compelled to eat matza fulfills the duty.
Who compelled the person?
Insanity cannot be the case, since a person in that state is exempt.
Rav Ashi says the Persians compelled the eating.
Rava infers that a shofar blower seeking music still fulfills the duty.
Why is that inference needed?
Matza may be different because the commanded act is eating; the explanation continues on 28b.

28b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Even though shofar is called a memorial blast, the unintentional blower can fulfill it.
The Gemara identifies Rava’s view as mitzvot not requiring intent.
The Shema mishna seems to require intent to fulfill the reading.
Its intent can mean intent to read the words.
But the person is already reading.
The case is reading to correct a text rather than articulate it.
The mishna about hearing shofar from outside a synagogue also seems to require intent to fulfill.
The relevant intent is to hear the shofar.
But the listener already hears it.
The listener might mistake the sound for a donkey.
A baraita requires intent from both listener and blower.
A listener lacking intent may simply mistake the sound for a donkey.
A blower playing music would still fail under the baraita.
Perhaps the blower made only bark-like noises, not proper blasts.
Abaye asks whether sleeping in a sukkah on the eighth day then violates the ban on adding.
Rava limits an unintentional addition to the mitzva’s prescribed time.
A baraita forbids a priest to add his own blessing under the ban on adding to the command.
That addition can occur after the priest has completed the prescribed blessing.
Perhaps he had not yet finished.
Another baraita says he had finished.
That can mean only one of the blessings.
A further baraita says he finished all of them.
He may bless another congregation later, so the whole day remains the mitzva’s time.
What supports treating the whole day as the prescribed time?
A mishna first gives rules for mixed sacrificial blood with equal sprinkling counts.
Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua disagree when one- and four-sprinkling blood mix.
Rabbi Eliezer says one sprinkling unlawfully diminishes the four required.
Rabbi Yehoshua says four unlawfully add to the one required.
Rabbi Eliezer says adding applies only to blood standing alone.
Rabbi Yehoshua applies the same limit to diminishing.
Rabbi Yehoshua further prefers a passive omission to a positive act of adding.
The added sprinklings can violate even after the firstborn’s required sprinkling, suggesting the whole day remains available.
Perhaps Rabbi Yehoshua forbids adding even outside the proper time.
Why did Rav Shemen cite a baraita rather than this mishna?
Both blood sprinkling and priestly blessing can recur later that day.
How did Rav Shemen distinguish the two?
A new offering requires sprinkling, while blessing another congregation is optional.
Rava proposes that fulfilling needs no intent but violating the ban on adding does.
Rabbi Yehoshua’s blood ruling seems to forbid adding without such intent.
Rava distinguishes additions in a mitzva’s time, which need no intent, from additions outside it.
Rabbi Zeira begins an instruction to his servant that continues on 29a.

29a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Zeira asks the blower to intend to sound for him, implying the blower’s intent matters.
The passerby mishna seems to require only the listener’s intent, not the blower’s intent for him.
The blower there is the community’s representative, intending for everyone.
A baraita seems to accept a blower intending for himself without specifically intending for the listener.
This is a tannaitic dispute; Rabbi Yosei requires both intents for a private blower.
The mishna cites the verse about Moses raising his hands during battle.
Did Moses’s hands themselves win or lose the war?
Israel prevailed when they looked upward and directed their hearts to Heaven.
The mishna cites the fiery serpent raised on a pole.
Did the serpent itself kill or heal?
Healing followed when the people looked upward and directed their hearts to Heaven.
The mishna says one not obligated cannot fulfill the shofar duty for others.
A baraita lists those obligated to hear shofar, including priests and people of uncertain status.
It distinguishes whose obligation a tumtum, an androginos, or a half-free person can discharge.
Why explicitly list priests, Levites, and Israelites as obligated?
One might think priests’ trumpet sounding throughout the year exempts them from the day’s blast.
Their annual instruments are trumpets, whereas this mitzva uses shofar.
A different concern links Rosh HaShana to Jubilee rules from which priests differ.
The baraita’s half-slave rule is recalled.
Rav Huna allows such a person to sound for himself.
Rav Naḥman argues that his slave side cannot discharge his own free side either.
Rav Naḥman therefore disallows even sounding for himself.
A baraita explicitly confirms that restriction.
A baraita distinguishes blessings one may repeat for others from bread and wine blessings of enjoyment.
Rava begins a question that continues on 29b.

29b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Can one who already fulfilled the mitzva recite the matza or kiddush blessing for another?
Rav Pappi recited kiddush again for his workers after reciting it for his students.
A baraita limits blessing over bread for guests but allows teaching one’s household.
One who already fulfilled Hallel or Megilla may still fulfill it for others.
The text closes the preceding chapter.
The mishna describes Shabbat shofar sounding in the Temple and the later court enactment.
Rabbi Elazar limits the enactment to Yavne; the other Sages include any court.
The mishna contrasts Jerusalem’s neighboring cities with sounding only at Yavne’s court.
What is the source for the Shabbat distinction?
Two verses speak of remembering blasts and of a day of sounding.
One proposed reading distinguishes Shabbat from a weekday.
Rava objects that a Torah ban could not permit Temple sounding and that sounding is not labor.
A teaching excludes shofar sounding and removing bread from prohibited labor.
Rava attributes the Shabbat limit to a decree against carrying the horn to an expert.
The same carrying concern applies to lulav and Megilla.
The enactment is recalled, followed by a baraita about a Shabbat gathering in Yavne.
Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai proposes sounding the horn.
The sons of Beteira ask to discuss it first.
He says to sound first and discuss afterward.
After the sounding they renew the request to discuss.
He says a completed public act cannot now be overturned.
The mishna’s dispute over Yavne and other courts is recalled.
How do the final Sages differ from the first tanna?
Their difference concerns a temporary court.
The court rule is restated before the next discussion.
Rav Huna begins a teaching continued on 30a.

30a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Huna’s rule is that Shabbat sounding occurs with the court.
What does “with the court” mean?
It requires sounding in the court’s presence.
Rava tests that limit against Jerusalem’s additional advantage over Yavne.
What is the additional advantage?
One possibility is that individuals sound in Jerusalem but not Yavne.
A report of many individual blasts in Yavne refutes that possibility.
The alternative of sounding during court hours, even away from it, challenges Rav Huna.
Jerusalem differs because sounding was allowed away from the court; Yavne requires its presence.
Another tradition places Rav Huna’s rule alongside the Jubilee command to each individual.
What does “with the court” mean in that tradition?
It limits sounding to the hours when the court sits.
Rava cites a baraita permitting Shabbat sounding by every man and his house.
Does “man and house” mean wife, though women are exempt from this time-bound duty?
Perhaps it permits a man to sound at home even outside court hours.
The permission still applies only during court hours.
Rav Sheshet cites a baraita contrasting Jubilee and Rosh HaShana courts and individuals.
Does it deny individual sounding on Rosh HaShana entirely?
The report from Yavne confirms that individuals sounded there.
Reading the baraita as allowing Jubilee sounding after court hours challenges Rav Huna.
Both require court hours; Jubilee permits sounding outside its presence, Rosh HaShana does not.
A reported teaching also limits sounding to the period when the court is seated.
If judges prepare to rise but remain seated, is that still court time? The issue remains unresolved.
The mishna’s rule about towns near Jerusalem is recalled.
The sight requirement excludes a town in a valley.
The hearing requirement excludes a town on a mountaintop.
The nearness requirement excludes one beyond the Shabbat boundary.
The ability to come excludes a town cut off by a river.
The mishna records seven-day lulav and full-day new-grain restrictions after the Temple’s destruction.
What is the basis for commemorating the Temple?
Jeremiah’s call to care for Zion supports acts of remembrance.
The new-grain enactment is recalled.
Why prohibit new grain for the whole day?
A rebuilt Temple could lead people to eat at dawn, unaware the omer offering must first permit it.
If rebuilding occurs on the sixteenth, would not dawn already permit the grain?
If rebuilding precedes the sixteenth, why not allow eating by midday after the offering?
A late or nighttime rebuilding could delay the offering beyond midday.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak begins another explanation on 30b.

30b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Naḥman links the full-day new-grain rule to Rabbi Yehuda’s reading of “until this very day.”
Does Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai really agree with Rabbi Yehuda?
In the mishna Rabbi Yehuda objects that the new grain was already forbidden by Torah law.
Rabbi Yehuda misunderstood the enactment; both readings may treat the ban as Torah law.
The mishna calls it an institution, which sounds rabbinic.
The institution can mean interpreting the verse and establishing its practice.
The new mishna recalls the earlier practice of accepting moon testimony all day.
After late witnesses disrupted the Levites’ song, acceptance was limited to afternoon prayer time and two holy days could result.
After the Temple’s destruction, Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai restored all-day acceptance.
What went wrong in the Levites’ song?
One interpretation says they sang no psalm.
Rabbi Zeira says they sang the ordinary weekday psalm at the afternoon offering.
A baraita describes leaving enough time for offerings and the correct song.
The term “error” seems to imply an incorrect song rather than no song.
Failing to sing anything would itself be a severe error.
A baraita gives the usual morning, festival additional, and afternoon psalms.
When Rosh HaShana is Thursday, the morning song changes to avoid repeating the festival psalm.
The morning song then begins with “I removed his shoulder from the burden.”
If witnesses arrive after the morning offering, the festival song is repeated anyway.
That repetition suggests the weekday song was sung while the new-month status was uncertain.

31a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Thursday psalm applies to that day even before the new-month status is known.
Rabbi Yehuda reports the first day’s psalm and its link to creation.
The second day’s psalm recalls the division of creation.
The third day’s psalm recalls the revealed land and prepared world.
The fourth day’s psalm concerns the created sun and moon.
The fifth day’s psalm recalls birds and fish praising God.
The sixth day’s psalm recalls completion of creation.
The Shabbat psalm is linked here to a future entirely at rest.
Rabbi Neḥemya asks why the seventh psalm is read differently from the first six.
He repeats the creation links and reads the seventh psalm as the first Shabbat.
The readings are linked to Rav Ketina’s teaching about a future desolate period.
Isaiah’s verse speaks of God alone being exalted on that day.
Abaye offers a two-period reading and cites Hosea.
What was sung with the additional Shabbat offering?
Rav gives the six-part Ha’azinu mnemonic.
The same sections govern the synagogue reading.
What was sung with the afternoon Shabbat offering?
Rabbi Yoḥanan names portions of the Sea Song and Well Song.
Were all sections sung each Shabbat or one section per week?
A baraita’s comparison of six and three sections supports one per week.
Rabbi Yoḥanan pairs ten journeys of the Divine Presence with ten moves of the Sanhedrin.
The stages of the Divine Presence’s departure are listed from the Ark cover to its own place.
Verses support the moves among the Ark cover, cherubs, and threshold.
Further verses trace the moves through the courtyard, altar, roof, wall, and city.
Verses trace the moves from the city to the mountain, wilderness, and beyond.
Rabbi Yoḥanan says the Presence lingered in the wilderness awaiting repentance.
A verse about lost hope accompanies the account of its departure.
The parallel list of the Sanhedrin’s moves begins with the Chamber, Ḥanut, Jerusalem, and Yavne.

31b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Sanhedrin’s moves conclude at Tiberias, described as the lowest point.
Isaiah’s verse about speaking low from the earth supports that image.
Rabbi Elazar counts six exiles by location.
A verse gives repeated expressions of descent.
Rabbi Yoḥanan says redemption will emerge from that low point.
Isaiah calls Zion to rise from the dust.
The mishna sends moon witnesses to the fixed meeting place even if the head of court is elsewhere.
Ameimar summons a woman who does not follow him when he moves, and sanctions her.
Rav Ashi challenges him with the mishna’s rule against following the head of court.
Ameimar limits that rule to moon witnesses, whose future willingness must be protected.
A baraita bars priests from the blessing platform in sandals and counts this among nine enactments.
Six enactments are in this chapter and one in the first.
A convert’s set-aside offering money is another rule later rescinded to avoid misuse.
Rav Pappa and Rav Naḥman disagree whether the ninth concerns fourth-year fruit or crimson wool.
The fourth-year fruit rule required produce near Jerusalem to be brought there.
Why require the nearby fruit to come to Jerusalem?
It adorned the city markets with fruit.
Rabbi Eliezer considers making his fourth-year fruit ownerless after the destruction.
His students say the rule was already lifted; the account identifies Rabban Yoḥanan as the author.
Rav Naḥman instead identifies the crimson strip as the ninth enactment.
The strip was first placed outside, then inside the Temple entrance to spare public distress.
When people still peeked, the strip was moved to a rock and the scapegoat.
Why does Rav Naḥman reject the fruit enactment?
Rabban Yoḥanan was Rabbi Eliezer’s teacher, not his colleague as the students said.
Rav Pappa says students avoid calling their own teacher another teacher’s pupil.
Why does Rav Pappa reject the crimson-strip enactment?
He questions whether its Temple-era timing fits Rabban Yoḥanan’s career.
A baraita divides Rabban Yoḥanan’s life into commerce, study, and teaching.
Another source places the strip’s failure in the final forty Temple years, before his later enactments.
Rav Naḥman says he could have proposed the rule while still a student.

32a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabban Yoḥanan’s teacher later established that proposed rule in his name.
Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri places Kingship with the opening blessings and sounds after the later themes.
Rabbi Akiva asks why mention Kingship if no blast follows it.
He places Kingship with the day’s sanctification and sounds after it.
The Gemara repeats Rabbi Akiva’s challenge to mentioning Kingship.
Mentioning Kingship itself is required.
Why recite ten Kingship verses if it has a different blast arrangement?
Its altered arrangement could justify a different count.
A baraita cites psalm verses for the opening blessings.
What is the source for Kingship, Remembrances, and Shofarot?
Rabbi Eliezer reads the festival verse as giving the day, memory, blasts, and sacred observance.
Rabbi Akiva objects to assigning the opening word to the day’s blessing.
He reads that word as rest and the closing phrase as the day’s sanctification.
Where is the source for Kingship?
Rabbi reads God’s declaration before the seventh-month passage as Kingship.
Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda reads the extra divine title beside Remembrance as a model for Kingship.
Where is the day’s sanctification recited?
Rabbi joins it to Kingship in the fourth blessing, matching the usual place.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel joins it to Remembrances in the middle blessing.
At Usha, one prayer leader follows Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri and is corrected.
The next leader follows Rabbi Akiva and receives approval for the Yavne practice.
Does Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel then hold like Rabbi Akiva?
They place the day’s sanctification with different blessings.
The agreement concerns sounding a blast for Kingship.
Does “the second day” imply an unusually full Elul?
A teaching says no full Elul was found since Ezra’s days.
It means Rosh HaShana the following year.
The mishna requires ten verses for each theme; Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri accepts three.
What do the ten Kingship verses represent?
One answer links them to ten praises in Psalms.
Psalms contains many more praises.
The count points to the praises in the shofar psalm.
Rav Yosef links the count to the Ten Commandments.
Rabbi Yoḥanan links it to ten utterances of creation.
There are only nine explicit “And God said” passages.
The opening “In the beginning” also counts as an utterance, supported by a psalm.
Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri’s three-verse allowance is recalled.
Does that mean three from each scriptural division or one from each?
A baraita describes ten as standard and seven as sufficient.
It specifies three total for Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri, tied to the three scriptural divisions.
Shmuel rules like Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri.
The next mishna excludes punitive verses and discusses where the sequence begins and ends.

32b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A verse about God reigning in anger is excluded from Kingship verses.
Rav Naḥman welcomes even divine anger if it brings redemption.
Its angry setting still makes it unsuitable to mention on Rosh HaShana.
A punitive remembrance verse is likewise excluded.
A shofar verse describing calamity is also excluded.
Punishment directed at other nations may be cited in all three themes.
Two psalms provide examples of Kingship over hostile nations.
The remembrance of Edom supplies a permitted remembrance verse.
Zechariah couples God’s shofar blast with protection of Israel.
Personal remembrance verses are excluded even when favorable.
Rabbi Yosei counts divine visitation verses as remembrances.
Rabbi Yehuda does not count visitation as remembrance.
Sarah’s visitation appears to concern one individual, contrary to the rule.
Her many descendants make her visitation collective in effect.
Psalm 24 repeatedly calls God the King of glory.
Rabbi Yosei counts two Kingship references in its first section and three in the second.
Rabbi Yehuda counts only one in the first section and two in the second.
Psalm 47 includes both “our King” and “King of all the earth.”
Rabbi Yosei counts both references.
Rabbi Yehuda counts just one of them.
Both count the verse about God reigning over nations as one Kingship verse.
Rabbi Yosei allows a remembrance verse with a blast in both relevant sections.
Rabbi Yehuda assigns that verse only to Remembrances.
Rabbi Yosei allows a Kingship verse with a blast in Kingship and Shofarot.
Rabbi Yehuda assigns that verse only to Kingship.
Rabbi Yosei allows a bare blast verse in Shofarot.
Rabbi Yehuda rejects such a verse entirely.
The mishna states the order of Torah and prophetic verses and Rabbi Yosei’s alternative.
Does “if he concluded” imply that Torah at the end is only valid after the fact?
A baraita praises concluding with Torah.
The proposed reading makes Torah the proper ending.
The mishna’s actual conditional wording still appears to say otherwise.
Rabbi Yosei prefers Torah at the end but accepts a prophetic ending after the fact.
A baraita records that the scrupulous concluded with Torah.
How can Kingship end with a Torah verse when only three such verses are apparent and ten are needed?
Rav Huna cites a dispute counting the Shema as a Kingship verse.
Rabbi Yosei also counts the declaration that God alone is God; Rabbi Yehuda disagrees.
A second declaration of God’s uniqueness yields the same dispute.
The mishna assigns the Rosh HaShana blast to the later leader and Hallel to the earlier leader.
If a larger congregation explains the later blast, why is Hallel not also later?
If prompt performance explains early Hallel, why is the blast not also early?
Rabbi Yoḥanan attributes the delayed blast to a period of persecution.
The mishna implies no Hallel is recited on Rosh HaShana; why?
The angels ask why Israel omits song on days of judgment.
God says the open books of life and death make joyous song unfitting.
The mishna prohibits transgressing festival restrictions to obtain or prepare a shofar.
Water or wine may nevertheless be placed inside the shofar.
Children may practice sounding the shofar with adult guidance.
An unintentional blower and a listener to that blower do not fulfill the obligation.
Why may shofar sounding not override festival restrictions?
The positive shofar command does not override both the festival prohibition and its positive rest command.
Why list Torah level concerns after already excluding rabbinic restrictions?
The mishna lists the stronger case after the weaker one for emphasis.

33a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna bars preparing a shofar with tools subject to either rabbinic or Torah prohibitions.
A sickle illustrates the lesser restriction and a knife the Torah prohibition.
Why specify the stronger ban once the lesser ban is already stated?
The mishna lists the lesser case and then the obvious stronger one.
Water or wine may be poured into the shofar.
Does the wording exclude urine, and whose teaching is this?
Abba Shaul permits water or wine for clarity but excludes urine out of respect.
The mishna allows children to practice shofar sounding.
Does this imply women are stopped, despite a baraita allowing them to sound it?
Abaye attributes the two teachings to different tannaitic views.
Rabbi Yehuda reads the offering verse as excluding women from laying hands.
Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon permit women to lay hands voluntarily.
The mishna instructs adults to practice with children.
Rabbi Elazar includes Shabbat in that instruction.
A baraita allows teaching and does not stop children sounding even on Shabbat.
Teaching actively seems to invite children to sound, while merely not stopping them suggests no invitation.
The Gemara begins distinguishing the cases; the answer continues on the next daf.

33b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Active instruction applies to a child of training age; a younger child is merely not stopped.
An unintentional shofar blower does not fulfill the command.
Does this imply a musician fulfills the command, supporting Rava?
A musician may also fall under the mishna’s unintentional category.
A listener to an unintentional blower does not fulfill the command.
Does a listener to a blower acting for himself fulfill it, against Rabbi Zeira’s instruction?
The second clause may repeat the unintentional case without addressing a blower acting for himself.
The mishna specifies three sets of blasts and the durations of tekia and terua.
A lengthened closing tekia counts as only one blast.
One who receives a shofar after prayer sounds the threefold sequence three times.

Rabban Gamliel says the prayer leader discharges the congregation’s obligation.
A baraita gives the tekia and terua equal length, apparently contradicting the mishna.
Abaye says the mishna compares all three sets together while the baraita compares one set.
The mishna makes a terua the length of three whimpers.
A baraita instead gives it the length of three broken sighs.
Abaye says these sources truly disagree.

The other understands it as short cries.

The shared seventh-month term supports a verbal analogy.

Why does the teaching switch from juxtaposition to verbal analogy?
The analogy supersedes a juxtaposition that would otherwise have sufficed.
Another tanna derives the pattern from wilderness blasts.
The wilderness verse names a tekia and terua separately.
Could the two terms describe one combined sound?
A gathering verse distinguishes tekia from terua.
What requires a tekia before terua?
The wording puts a tekia before a terua.
What requires a tekia after terua?
Another verse places a tekia after the terua.
Rabbi Yishmael derives the following tekia from the otherwise extra word “second.”
How does this wilderness pattern apply to Rosh HaShana?
The shared word terua supports a verbal analogy.
Three verses supply three teruot in the Rosh HaShana sequence.
Each terua has two accompanying tekiot, for nine sounds altogether.
One view counts two teruot as Torah law and the third as an interpretive addition.
Rabbi Yonatan counts one as Torah law and two as interpretive additions.
What independent purpose has the verse “day of terua”?
It requires sounding by day rather than at night.
Where does the first tanna learn the daytime rule?
He derives it from the Jubilee Day of Atonement.
Why not also learn the accompanying tekiot from that Jubilee verse?
For this tanna its proclamation words have another use.
What use do those words have?
Rav Mattana reads one as requiring the shofar in its natural orientation.
The second word precludes carrying the shofar without sounding it.
How does the other tanna derive Rav Mattana’s rule?
The unusual change of wording teaches it.
Could the verse still mean simply carrying the shofar by hand?
A verbal analogy to Moses’s audible proclamation shows that sounding is required.
Would analogy to the wilderness also require trumpets at Rosh HaShana?
A psalm specifically prescribes shofar on the festival at the covered moon.
Which festival has the moon concealed?
Rosh HaShana calls for a shofar.
Rabbi Abbahu institutes tekia, three shevarim, terua, tekia.
Why combine shevarim and terua if either alone could be the required cry?
He is unsure whether the prescribed cry is a sigh or a wail.

A separate tekia-terua-tekia sequence covers that possibility.

A separate tekia-shevarim-tekia sequence covers that possibility.
Why retain the combined sequence if each individual possibility is already covered?
Perhaps the required cry combines sighing and wailing.

A distressed person ordinarily sighs before wailing.
The mishna’s extended second tekia is recalled.

Outside a congregation only the blast order is required.

If towns offer only one or the other, travel to the town sounding the shofar.

The mishna’s dispute over individual and leader prayer obligations is recalled.

Field workers face constraints that absent townspeople do not.
